title: The Rebrand You Don’t Announce
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder writes from inside a transition rather than after it, describing her decision to step away from the business she had been known for without a launch, a rebrand announcement or a polished redemption arc. The piece's honesty is its method: she names the breakdown that preceded the decision, the years spent keeping a company alive for the version of herself who had created it, and her husband's earlier and clearer sight of what she needed. She traces how the drive to prove something led her to stack offer on offer and buy into every guru and high-ticket programme on the internet, and reports being their best student before it broke anyway. The financial and human cost is stated plainly, including closers who grew addicted to commission and sold to clients the promise was never meant for. Her accountability is total: she built the machine, let it run and kept showing up for it while it bled out. What she proposes instead is a reputation rooted in integrity rather than visibility and a practice of speaking while the questions still outweigh the answers. The closing admission that rebuilding feels like grief, because you mourn the parts of you that earned applause, gives the essay its edge.
points: Mulder's central distinction is between a business that no longer fits and a self that no longer fits, and she argues the second is what actually forces the exit.
The observation that the parts of the business she fought hardest for were precisely the parts that broke, while the true parts survived, is the essay's sharpest self-indictment.
She locates the failure of her sales machine not in the closers but in the promise itself, which was never meant for the inexperienced clients desperation pushed them to sell to.
Writing publicly mid-mess rather than after the case study is presented as a deliberate positioning choice, on the grounds that connection lives in the unresolved present.
The claim that rebuilding feels like grief, because you lose the version of you that made other people feel safe, reframes reinvention as a loss rather than an upgrade.
quotes: I spent years building something I convinced myself was my dream, only to realize I was keeping it alive for the version of me that created it… not the one I’d become.
Because for years, I was trying to look like the leader I already was while quietly questioning everything behind the scenes.
Every guru. Every high-ticket coaching program. Every marketing system that promised a ten x return if I just followed the damn steps.
Closers got addicted to commission checks. They sold to the wrong people. They made promises we couldn’t deliver on.
So right now, I’m doing something most people advise against. I’m letting you in while the wounds are still open. While I’m still cleaning up the mess.
I’m not looking to go viral. I’m not looking to be noticed. I’m looking to take the pain and turn it into impact that is undeniable.
